newsitem.title: USA: Japan MOF will guard against excessively weak yen.
newsitem.headline: Japan MOF will guard against excessively weak yen.

text.p: A senior Japanese Finance Ministry official said that Japan will stress at a G7 meeting on Sunday that G7 cooperation is important for currency stability.
The official told reporters that Japan will tell G7 members that excessive weakness of the yen is undesirable and Japan will act decisively against any such weakness.
The official said Japan will continue to pursue economic policies aimed at achieving growth led by domestic demand.
The United States has called on Japan to seek strong domestic demand-led growth to absorb more imports, helping cut Japan's huge trade surplus with the United States.
"Japan will make its currency stance clear, that excessive yen weakness as well as excessive yen strength is undesirable, and it will decisively deal with such moves," the official said.
Japan will not take short-term measures to envigorate economic activity, but will take medium- and long-term steps such as reforms of the fiscal and financial systems, he said.
"We want the United States to pay attention to Japan's medium- and long-term policies," he said.
Asked if the G7 will issue a statement on Sunday that contains stronger wording on currency stability than its Berlin statement in February, the official said it depends on how G7 discussion goes.
"The matter (of wording) may be brought up at a meeting of Finance Minister (Hiroshi) Mitsuzuka and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin," the official said.

The G7, in an unsual move, had issued a statement on currencies in Berlin, saying that major misalignments in exchange markets noted in its April 1995 communique had been corrected. It said that G7 members would monitor developments in foreign exchange markets and cooperate, as appropriate.
Mitsuzuka, who arrived in Washington on Saturday afternoon, is scheduled to meet Rubin and German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Sunday ahead of the G7 meeting.
The Group of Seven industrialized countries includes Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
The official said Japan will also tell G7 members that the problem of non-performing loans held by Japanese financial institutions is being handled effectively.
Japan's Finance Ministry is helping financial institutions that are making efforts to their restructure businesses, the official said.
"A stable financial system in Japan will contribute to stability of financial systems in the world," he said.
Rubin has urged Japan to press ahead with its efforts to shore up its banking system, warning that any delay would only increase the costs of resolving the problem.
Japanese banks are saddled with billions of dollars in bad loans, a legacy of the collapse of the property market after the asset bubble of the late 1980s.
